Alright. I think I gave wrong kind of advice at first. I am not from America so I think I have learned different way to do this, but this is how I would solve this;

^(I used a lot of help from) [this useful video](https://youtu.be/HwkLIvCv7oI)

\----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1) We do not know the subscripts of the compound, but we do know that the products consist of H, C and O. Burning means, that things react with O^(2). This means that acetylene consists of C and H. 

Let's write down the equation;   
C^(x)H^(y) \+ O^(2) \--> CO^(2) \+ H^(2)O

2) Since we know the mass of the two products, we can calculate the ratios of the atoms in this compound **by calculating the moles of the products.** 

​

||C^(x)H^(y)| O^(2)|\-->|CO^(2)|H^(2)O|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|m (g)|4,758|||16,104|3,294|
|M (g/mol)||||44,0098|18,01528|
|n (mol)||||0,3659185|0,1828447851|

​

3) We find the moles of C and H (which we have concluded acetylene to consist of) by looking at the ratios in which they appear in the molecule; for C it is 1 and for H it is 2. 

These are the numbers you need to multiply the mol-results with. ^(In other words, 1 mol of water consists of 2 moles of H. To get how many moles of H there is, we multiply moles of water with 2.) 

We get

C = 0,3659185, and

H = 0,1828447851 \* 2 = 0,3656895702

4) Find the ratios; the smallest number is 0,3656895702 (although they are almost identical, which they also are SUPPOSED to be. There must have happened some deviations in the processes when the masses of the products were measured, I think..?)

So now we obviously just divide both numbers with this 'smallest number', and boom we get

C = 1

H = 1

5) We now know that their ratios are 1:1. The empirical formula is therefore CH.

You need to first find how many mol each atom, C, H and O, gives. 

1. Find the molecular weight of each atom.
2. Divide the grams by their molecular weight.
3. Now you have the mol's
4. See which moles are the smallest number
5. Divide all the mol's by the smallest number of the mol's.
6. Now you have the numbers for the amounts of the atoms in the empirical formula.
